claim: GitHub engineering (undated, self-reported): merge trains of up to 15 PRs often derailed, and developers sometimes waited 8+ hours for a train to ship, only to have their change removed for a conflict.

GitHub engineering (undated, self-reported) states the principle that conflicting or build-breaking changes must not hold up all other queued PRs, and that system throughput is favoured over fairness to one PR.

GitHub engineering (undated, self-reported): after its merge queue, over 500 engineers merged 2,500 pull requests a month into the monorepo and the average wait to ship a change fell by 33 %; no absolute wait time or baseline is given.
note: The 33 % is the only wait figure in the source; it has no baseline and no batch size or failure rate.

claim: GitHub engineering (undated, self-reported): before general availability the merge queue shipped 30,000+ pull requests with 4.5 million associated CI runs; the CI runs cover all checks, not one serial check.
Shopify engineering (undated, self-reported): Merge Queue v2 uses batches of 8 PRs, because larger batches raise theoretical throughput but make failures harder to isolate and increase rollbacks.
Shopify engineering (undated, self-reported): Merge Queue v2 runs CI on 3 batches of pull requests at any given time.
Shopify engineering (undated, self-reported): Shopify changes 40 times a day and merges about 400 commits to master daily.
Shopify engineering (undated, self-reported): over 90 % of pull requests to the core app use the merge queue (v1 introduction post).

Shopify engineering (undated, self-reported): a PR is removed only after failures exceed a tolerance, because legitimate failures propagate to all later CI runs while flaky tests do not block later runs.

Shopify engineering (undated, self-reported) table: for an assumed 25 % flake rate, false removal of a PR is 6.25 %, 1.5 %, 0.39 % and 0.097 % after 2, 3, 4 and 5 failures in a row; they chose a tolerance of 3, so removal comes on the 4th consecutive failure.
note: The 25 % is the source's example, not its measured flake rate. The values were read in order from a text strip whose table labels were lost, so the mapping to 2 to 5 failures is not confirmed against the page.

claim: Shopify engineering (undated, self-reported): a v1 merge queue with upwards of 50 pull requests could take hours to merge and deploy; no later figure for that case is given.
Rust project rustc-dev-guide (self-reported): bors tests one PR at a time, and with a full CI run of about 2 hours the maximum merged in a day is 'around ~10'.
note: The source's line numbers for these quotes are approximate to within two. No failure rate is given.

claim: Rust project rustc-dev-guide (self-reported): it can take several hours until all automatic CI jobs finish.
Rust project rustc-dev-guide (self-reported): rollups merge several pending trivial PRs to be tested together; a team member builds them by hand and decides by judgment whether a PR is risky.
note: No rollup size or gain is given.

claim: Chromium Commit Queue docs (self-reported): a builder should have median cycle time under 40 minutes and a 90th percentile around an hour; this is a requirement for a builder to join, not a measured figure.
Chromium Commit Queue docs (self-reported): the CQ has roughly 20,000 unique flaky tests, and without retries almost no change would pass it.
Chromium Commit Queue docs (self-reported): retries raise the chance a flaky test lands on tip of tree only sublinearly, but cut its effect on unrelated changes exponentially.
Chromium Commit Queue docs (self-reported): a builder must catch enough failures to be worth adding, and one that fails about once every couple of weeks is probably not worth adding.
Chromium Commit Queue docs (self-reported): a passing build can be reused for up to 24 hours, or within a window such as 800 commits.

Chromium Commit Queue docs (self-reported): a smaller curated test set optimises turnaround and still catches most but not all regressions, while a Mega CQ with far more tests runs for risky changes regardless of cycle time.
Kubernetes Tide docs (self-reported): Tide automatically runs batch tests and merges multiple PRs together whenever possible.
note: No batch size, gain or failure rate appears in these pages.

claim: Kubernetes Tide maintainers' guide: each merge to a pool invalidates the tests running for that pool and sends all other PRs in it back to Queued for retest.
note: A statement of cost, not a measurement.

claim: Kubernetes Tide maintainers' guide: Tide prioritises batches over individual PRs and merges an individual PR only if its batch fails.

Mozilla tree closure docs (policy, no numbers): patches land on a shared integration branch that is continuously tested, and the branch is closed to new pushes while sheriffs back out a failing change.
note: Policy only: no closure rate, backout rate or batch size is given.
